tagline: A personal note from the elder to his friend Gaius, praising his hospitality to traveling missionaries and confronting Diotrephes, a church leader who loves to be first.
overview:
Third John is the shortest book in the New Testament by word count, and the most personal of John's letters. It is a private note from the elder to a man named Gaius, whom he loves in the truth. Traveling Christian workers have come back to the elder with good reports: Gaius has welcomed them, fed them, and sent them on their way, even though they were strangers to him. The elder commends this and urges him to keep doing it, because those who support such workers become fellow workers for the truth.

The letter also names a problem. Diotrephes, a leader in the church, loves to be first. He has refused the elder's letter, spread malicious talk against him, turned away the traveling brothers, and even put out of the church those who wanted to welcome them. The elder promises to deal with it when he comes. Meanwhile he commends a man named Demetrius, who very likely carried the letter.

The letter is precious for what it shows of ordinary church life at the end of the first century: travel, hospitality, money, letters, rivalries, and friendships. It shows truth and love not as abstractions but as the way believers treat strangers and handle power.
author: As in Second John, the writer calls himself the elder. Early tradition identified him with John the apostle, and the shared vocabulary of the three letters (truth, love, walking in the truth, testimony, seeing God) points to one author or circle. Some scholars identify the elder with a leader distinct from the apostle, perhaps the John the elder whom Papias mentions in the early second century. What is clear from the letter is that the elder had recognized standing over more than one congregation and expected his letters and messengers to be received, and that at least one local leader was now resisting that standing.
date: Usually dated with the other letters of John, late in the first century, around AD 85 to 100. Nothing in the letter fixes the date more precisely. It gives no sign of the doctrinal dispute that dominates First and Second John; the conflict here is about authority and hospitality.
setting:
Christian mission in the Roman world depended on hospitality. Inns were few, expensive, and often disreputable, so traveling teachers and missionaries relied on believers to house them and to send them on with supplies for the next stage. The elder notes that these workers went out for the sake of the Name and accepted nothing from the Gentiles (verse 7), meaning they did not take support from unbelievers, which set them apart from traveling philosophers and religious teachers who lived on public gifts. The Didache, a Christian manual of church practice from about the same era or a little later, gives rules for receiving traveling apostles and prophets, which shows how common and how open to abuse the system was.

We know nothing of Gaius, Diotrephes, or Demetrius beyond this letter. Gaius was one of the most common Roman names, and the New Testament mentions several men called Gaius; there is no good reason to identify this one with any of them. Whether Diotrephes held a formal office or simply dominated a house church is unclear. Scholars have read the conflict as a clash of personalities, a struggle between traveling and local leadership, or an early step toward the single presiding bishop found in the second century. The letter does not say, and it is wise not to claim more than it tells.
purpose: The elder writes to thank and encourage Gaius for his hospitality, to ask him to continue supporting traveling workers, to warn him about Diotrephes' conduct and signal that the elder will address it in person, and to commend Demetrius. Underneath these practical aims is a single conviction: walking in the truth shows itself in how believers welcome others.
story: Third John belongs to the same period and circle as First and Second John, the last years of the apostolic generation in the churches of Asia. It pairs naturally with Second John. There, the elder warns a church not to welcome teachers who deny Christ; here, he rebukes a leader who will not welcome teachers who serve Christ. Together they show a church learning to discern. The wider biblical story of hospitality lies behind it, from Abraham welcoming strangers at Mamre (Genesis 18) to Jesus' words that whoever receives those he sends receives him.
christ: Christ is not named in the letter by title, but he is present in the Name for whose sake the brothers went out (verse 7), a way early Christians referred to Jesus himself. The letter shows what life under that Name looks like: care for strangers, support for the gospel's messengers, and leadership that serves rather than seeks first place. Jesus taught that the greatest must be the servant of all, and Diotrephes' love of being first stands in plain contrast. The elder's standard, that the one who does good is of God (verse 11), echoes the teaching of First John that those born of God show the likeness of the Son.
reading: Read Third John as a real letter between real people, with its gaps and assumptions. Don't build theories on the names. The elder's opening wish that Gaius may prosper and be in good health (verse 2) followed the ordinary conventions of letters in that world, which often began with a wish for the recipient's health. It is a friend's warm greeting, not a promise that the faithful will be wealthy, and reading it as the latter is a common misuse. Notice too how the letter models conflict: the elder names the wrong plainly, plans to address it face to face, and refuses to let one domineering leader define the church.

structure.title: Greeting and joy
structure.summary: The elder greets Gaius, wishes him health, and rejoices at reports that he walks in the truth.

structure.title: Hospitality to the brothers
structure.summary: He commends Gaius for welcoming traveling workers who were strangers to him and urges him to send them on in a manner worthy of God.

structure.title: The problem of Diotrephes
structure.summary: Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder's authority, slanders him, refuses the brothers, and expels those who would welcome them.

structure.title: Imitate the good; Demetrius commended
structure.summary: Gaius should imitate the good, not the evil. Demetrius has a good testimony from all and from the truth itself.

structure.title: Closing
structure.summary: The elder hopes to visit soon and speak face to face, and sends and asks for greetings among friends.

themes.title: Hospitality as partnership
themes.body: By welcoming and supplying traveling workers, Gaius becomes a fellow worker for the truth. Hospitality in the early church was not a social nicety but a direct share in mission, and the letter treats it as one of the clearest expressions of love.

themes.title: Walking in the truth
themes.body: The elder's greatest joy is to hear that his children walk in the truth (verse 4). Truth is not only believed but lived, and in this letter it is lived in faithfulness to strangers and generosity to those who serve.

themes.title: The danger of loving first place
themes.body: Diotrephes is the Bible's brief portrait of a leader who treats the church as his own. He rejects outside accountability, controls who may be welcomed, and uses exclusion as a weapon. The letter names the sin plainly and does not excuse it because the man holds a position.

themes.title: Imitation and testimony
themes.body: Believers become like what they imitate. The elder urges Gaius to imitate the good, and he offers Demetrius as someone whose life is confirmed by many witnesses. Character in the church is a matter of public testimony, not private claims.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter: hospitality as partnership in the truth, and a warning against leadership that loves to be first.
